title: Percentages in Use
subtitle: Increase, decrease, and reading what a percentage is OF.
objectives: Work out a percentage increase and decrease
Explain why the starting amount matters
Find what percentage one number is of another

cards.title: The trap is always the same: a percentage of what?
cards.text: Ten per cent off and ten per cent on do not cancel out. Once you see why, most percentage mistakes disappear.

cards.title: Add the percentage to the original
cards.text: Work out the part, then add it. Or multiply once and save a step.
points: **Faster:** multiply by 1.2 directly.
**The 1 is the original.** The decimal is what you add.

cards.title: Take the percentage off
cards.text: Same move, going down. Multiply by what is left.
points: **20% off 50** → multiply by 0.8 → 40.
**'Off' means what remains**, so subtract from 1 first.
**Half price** is × 0.5, which is 50% off.

question.explain: ₱300 off, so ₱900 to pay. The two always add back to ₱1,200.

cards.title: Twenty out of a hundred
cards.alt: A ten-by-ten grid of cream wall tiles with two full columns, twenty tiles, in deep terracotta
cards.text: Count the dark ones. A percentage is a count out of a hundred, drawn.

cards.title: Press a discount
cards.text: Two bars on a ₱1,200 item. Watch them trade against each other.

cards.title: A new car loses about a fifth of its value in year one
cards.text: And then it loses a percentage of the smaller number next year. The drop gets gentler every time.
points: **Year two, another 20%** → but of 800,000, so ₱640,000.
**Not 400,000.** Each cut is from a smaller base.
**Same reason** up-then-down does not cancel.

question.text: A ₱500 item has 30% off. What do you pay?

cards.title: '110% effort' is a maths joke people make seriously
cards.text: Percentages over 100 are real, but not when the whole is a maximum you cannot pass.
points: **120% of a price** is fine. Prices have no ceiling.
**120% of a battery** is not. Full is the whole.
**Giving 110%** is hyperbole, like 'back in my day'.
**Ask what the whole is.** That decides whether it makes sense.

cards.title: Up 10% then down 10% is not where you started
cards.text: Each percentage is taken of a different number, and that is the whole reason.
points: **Now take 10% off 110** → that is 11, not 10.
**You land on 99.** Lower than you began.
**The second percentage was of a bigger number.**

question.text: A price rises 10%, then falls 10%. Compared with the start it is…
question.explain: The fall is taken from the raised price, so it removes more than the rise added. 100 → 110 → 99.

cards.title: What percentage is this of that?
cards.text: Divide the part by the whole, then multiply by 100.
points: **Part on top**, whole underneath. Always.
**Check it is sensible.** More than half should be over 50%.
**That is how a test score becomes a percentage.**

cards.title: A percentage with no number behind it is a trick
cards.text: 'Cases up 200%' sounds alarming. From one case to three is also 200%.
points: **Percentage change hides the size** it started from.
**Always ask for the raw number** as well.
**A small base** makes any change look enormous.
**Both numbers, or neither.**

terms.def: The amount added, as a percentage of the original.
The amount taken off, as a percentage of the original.
The single number you multiply by, like 1.2 or 0.8.
The amount the percentage is taken of.

cards.title: Twenty per cent, lifted off
cards.alt: A stack of ten blank coins with two lifted away and floating above it
cards.text: Ten coins, two taken away. That is the discount; the eight left are what you pay.

cards.title: What to remember
points: Increase: × (1 + the decimal). Decrease: × (1 − the decimal).
Up 10% then down 10% lands below the start.
One number as a percentage of another: part ÷ whole × 100.
A percentage change with no base behind it tells you very little.

quiz.text: A ₱800 jacket has 40% off. You pay…
quiz.objective: Percentages, and their relationships with fractions and decimals

quiz.text: A price goes up 10%, then down 10%. It is now…
quiz.explain: 100 → 110 → 99. The fall came off a bigger number.
quiz.objective: Percentages, and their relationships with fractions and decimals

quiz.text: What percentage is 18 out of 24? Digits only, no % sign.
quiz.objective: Percentages, and their relationships with fractions and decimals

quiz.text: You scored 36 out of 40. As a percentage that is…
quiz.objective: Percentages, and their relationships with fractions and decimals

quiz.text: Up 50% then down 50% returns you to the start.
quiz.explain: 100 → 150 → 75. The decrease is taken from the larger amount.
quiz.objective: Percentages, and their relationships with fractions and decimals

quiz.explain: The 1 keeps the original and the 0.05 adds five per cent.
quiz.objective: Percentages, and their relationships with fractions and decimals

quiz.text: Cases rise from 1 to 3. That is an increase of…
quiz.explain: The rise is 2, and 2 out of 1 is 200%. Which is why the base matters.
quiz.objective: Percentages, and their relationships with fractions and decimals

quiz.text: To find what percentage one number is of another you…
quiz.explain: Part on top, whole underneath, then scale to a hundred.
quiz.objective: Percentages, and their relationships with fractions and decimals

quiz.text: A ₱200 item rises 15%. What is the new price? Digits only.
quiz.explain: 15% of 200 is 30, so the new price is 230. Or × 1.15.
quiz.objective: Percentages, and their relationships with fractions and decimals

quiz.text: A percentage over 100 is always a mistake.
quiz.explain: Only when the whole is a fixed maximum. A price can rise 150% quite happily.
quiz.objective: Percentages, and their relationships with fractions and decimals

teacher.summary: Term 2 Week 2 Math, the second of the scope's two percentage weeks, moved on to change rather than repeating conversion. Multipliers are taught early because they collapse two steps into one and make the up-then-down trap arithmetically obvious. That trap gets its own idea card and its own checkpoint, since it is the single most common percentage error. The last lens is a numeracy habit rather than a calculation: a percentage change with no base behind it is close to meaningless, which is worth him carrying out of the subject entirely.
discussion: Why does up 10% then down 10% not cancel?
When is a percentage over 100 nonsense?
Why do you need the raw number as well as the percentage?
extension: Find a sale sign and work out the real price before looking at it.
Find a headline percentage in the news and go looking for the base.
misconceptions: Taking the percentage of the wrong number.
